Professional interpretation was associated with better patient-reported understanding of diagnosis or treatment in 10 of the 14 studies. In three studies that recorded and coded encounters, clinically significant errors occurred in 22 percent of utterances interpreted by ad hoc interpreters and 12 percent of those interpreted by professionals. Outcome measures varied widely and most studies were small and observational, so results were not pooled."},{"title":"Remote video versus in-person interpretation: a systematic review of accuracy, satisfaction and patient understanding","authors":"Okonjo-Varga P, Nakashima-Ruiz E","year":2021,"venue":"Remote Interpreting Studies","doi":"10.5555/tsr.2021.0240","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 11 studies comparing remote video interpretation with in-person interpretation in hospital and clinic settings. Accuracy of interpretation and patient satisfaction were similar between modes in most studies. Patient-reported understanding was measured in only three small studies, which found no clear difference but could not exclude a meaningful one. Connection or equipment problems interrupted between 9 and 18 percent of video sessions where this was reported. No included study was designed to show that video and in-person interpretation are equivalent for understanding."},{"title":"Language barriers without interpretation and hospital outcomes: a meta-analysis","authors":"Achebe-Sorensen T, Grieve-Kowalski A, Ferreira-Iwu N","year":2019,"venue":"Language Access Evidence Notes","doi":"10.5555/hee.2019.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled 21 observational studies of hospitalised adults with limited proficiency in the language of care. Patients who did not receive professional interpretation had higher odds of readmission within 30 days (odds ratio 1.3, 95 percent CI 1.1 to 1.6) and longer stays than those who did. Heterogeneity was high and confounding by illness severity and socioeconomic position was likely. Patient-reported understanding was not an outcome in any included study. The authors caution that interpreter use may mark better-resourced wards rather than cause better outcomes."},{"title":"Interpreter use and understanding of informed consent: a systematic review","authors":"Petrov-Mensah L, Castillo-Lindgren S","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Language Access in Care","doi":"10.5555/jlac.2022.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 16 studies of consent discussions with patients who preferred a language other than that of the clinician. Understanding of consent information was measured in 7 studies, usually as recall of risks shortly after the discussion. Recall was better when a professional interpreter was present in five of these seven studies. Several studies found consent forms signed without any interpreter recorded. Most studies were cross-sectional and single-site, and none measured understanding more than a day after the consent discussion."},{"title":"Discharge instructions for patients with limited language proficiency: a scoping review","authors":"Harcourt-Obi D, Moreau-Tanaka K, Salazar-Holm B","year":2023,"venue":"Transitions of Care Studies","doi":"10.5555/tcs.2023.0056","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We charted 38 studies of discharge communication for patients with limited proficiency in the language of care. Interventions included professional interpretation at discharge, translated written instructions and teach-back. Patient-reported understanding was measured in only 9 of the 38 studies, and most studies reported satisfaction or clinician-reported delivery instead. Studies rarely described which interpreter mode was used, and fewer than half reported the languages of the patients included. The authors call for patient-reported understanding as a core outcome in this field and for reporting of interpreter mode and language in every study."},{"title":"Overlap and quality of reviews on medical interpreting: a methods study","authors":"Varadi-Adeyemi C, Lindgren-Whitcombe R","year":2024,"venue":"Evidence Synthesis Methods Notes","doi":"10.5555/esmn.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 19 reviews on medical interpreting published over 15 years and rated them with a critical appraisal tool for reviews. Three were rated high confidence and 11 critically low, most often because of missing protocols and no assessment of risk of bias in included studies. Primary studies overlapped substantially between reviews, with a corrected covered area of 18 percent, meaning that the same small studies were counted in many reviews. The authors recommend that overviews of this field account for overlap before drawing conclusions from the number of agreeing reviews."},{"title":"Bilingual staff as interpreters: language proficiency testing and interpretation errors","authors":"Mwangi-Holt S, Carvalho-Osei J","year":2014,"venue":"Language Access Evidence Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 12 studies of bilingual staff who interpreted for patients alongside their clinical roles. Staff who had passed a formal language proficiency test made fewer errors than untested staff, and in two studies their error rates approached those of professional interpreters. Untested bilingual staff often overestimated their proficiency. Few studies measured patient understanding, and none compared tested bilingual staff with professional interpreters on patient-reported outcomes. Most studies were small and from single hospitals, and the review's search ended more than a decade ago."}]}
